title: Leveraging AI for Hospital Resource Allocation: Validating the Risk Stratification Index (RSI 3.0) for Targeted Clinical Care
affiliations: Texas A&M University, affiliation not provided to SSRN and Houston Methodist Hospital

detail.title: Leveraging AI for Hospital Resource Allocation: Validating the Risk Stratification Index (RSI 3.0) for Targeted Clinical Care
detail.abstract: Background & Objectives:Hospital resource constraints necessitate efficient methods for identifying patients who will benefit the most from intensive transition-of-care programs. We assessed the external validity and clinical utility of the Risk Stratification Index 3.0 (RSI 3.0), a model trained on a large national Medicare dataset, for usage in a general inpatient setting.MethodsWe conducted a retrospective validation study of adult inpatient admissions (N = 38,715) at a Texas tertiary care hospital from January 2, 2023, to March 12, 2025. We evaluated the model’s discrimination (AUROC) and calibration for mortality and readmission. Additionally, we modeled the yield of a targeted intervention for the top 5% risk tier, comparing literature-based theoretical efficacy benchmarks against empirical 14-day outpatient follow-up data.ResultsDespite a younger cohort than the model’s training population (mean age 62 vs. 74), RSI 3.0 models demonstrated strong discrimination for 30-day post-discharge mortality (AUROC 0.81), inpatient mortality (AUROC 0.78), and 30-day readmission (AUROC 0.70). Intervening on the top 5% risk tier yielded high clinical efficiency. High-risk patients in our empirical model showed a 26.7% relative risk reduction in 30-day readmissions. This corresponds to an estimated Number Needed to Intervene (NNI) of 9.6 to prevent one readmission.ConclusionsThe RSI 3.0 validly stratifies risk in general inpatient populations regardless of demographic variations. AI-directed resource allocation can significantly reduce hospital readmissions and optimize efficiency through concentrated clinical interventions.

title: A multicenter validation of reference intervals derived indirectly using SOM-clean
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN, Yamaguchi University, affiliation not provided to SSRN, affiliation not provided to SSRN, Kawasaki University of Medical Welfare, Kawasaki University of Medical Welfare and affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title: A multicenter validation of reference intervals derived indirectly using SOM-clean
detail.abstract: Background & ObjectiveWe developed software named SOM-clean that enables derivation of reference intervals (RIs) from routine laboratory databases. It employs simultaneous analysis of multiple test results on a uniform scale and optimizes RIs through iterative data-cleaning guided by self-organizing map (SOM) clustering. Four university laboratories in Japan collaborated to assess the accuracy and reproducibility of SOM-clean RIs against the common RIs established in Japan, while a Turkish laboratory compared SOM-clean RIs with those derived directly from a nationwide study.MethodsRoutine laboratory data for 22 major health-screening tests (HSTs) and eight complete blood count (CBC) tests from each university were retrieved over a 2−6 year period after excluding results from patients tested multiple times. Because SOM-clean RIs depend on map size and parameter thresholds representing atypical multi-test patterns, optimal conditions were identified through a computationally intensive search based on overall goodness-of-fit of cleaned data to Gaussian distributions and conformity to reference RIs. For comparison, RIs were also estimated by refineR method recommended by IFCC. Reproducibility of SOM-clean RIs was expressed as the SD ratio (SDR), defined as the SD of RI limits across four laboratories divided by the average SD comprising their RIs. The accuracy of indirectly derived RIs was assessed as bias ratios (BRs) at the lower and upper RI limits relative to the reference RIs.ResultsSDR for between-laboratory differences in RIs by SOM-clean and refineR were within the conventional threshold of 0.40 in 77.3% and 64.8% among the HSTs, respectively. BRs of SOM-clean and refineR RIs from reference RIs were within the threshold of 0.50 in 78.4% and 44.3%, respectively. RIs by refineR frequently exhibited pronounced bias for tests with highly skewed distributions. Reproducibility of CBC RIs was improved by concurrent analysis with HSTs. SOM-clean RIs showed excellent agreement with directly derived Turkish RIs. The performance far exceeded that of refineR.ConclusionsThe reproducibility and accuracy of SOM-clean methods are at an acceptable level for deriving RIs for both HSTs and CBC tests. This method is a suitable tool for periodic validation of RIs as requested in ISO15189.
